catalog_quote: Stress has not fallen into a neat pattern for this analyst to date. Apparently I am not the first to have this difficulty as witness the following excerpts from Rule (1989:2) Stress is unpredictable... there is considerable fluctuation in where stress occurs in a number of words. a word may have the final syllable stressed... in isolation, but when that word occurs in an utterance the stress will shift, generally to the first syllable. Nevertheless, there are some generalizations that can be made. Let it be noted that stress does not seem to have a great deal of prominence. That is, there is not a great difference between stressed and unstressed syllables. No minimal stress pairs have been discovered to date. new_statements.quote: Stress has not fallen into a neat pattern for this analyst to date. [...] Let it be noted that stress does not seem to have a great deal of prominence. That is, there is not a great difference between stressed and unstressed syllables. No minimal stress pairs have been discovered to date. Stress also moves in a given word with the addition of suffixes. There does seem to be a tendency for heavy syllables to attract stress. [...] In two syllable words stress nearly always occurs on the first or penultimate syllable. [...] In three syllable words stress seems to vary between the penultimate and antepenultimate syllables with the former being slightly more common.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not predictable by rule (author concurs with Rule 1989 'unpredictable and in that sense therefore phonemic'), though no minimal pairs exist and prominence is weak. Tendencies: penultimate preferred; disyllables initial(=penult); trisyllables penult or antepenult; four-syllable words mostly penult, sometimes antepenult or initial; final stress only when the final syllable is heavy (CVV, e.g. verb + past -i diphthong); heavy CVV syllables tend to attract stress; stress position shifts as suffixes are added.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In long verbs (up to 10-12 syllables) primary stress is normally antepenultimate or penultimate and 'there appears to be a secondary stress every second or third syllable from the primary stress' (p.17, ex. 54).
new_statements.exceptions: Aspectual suffixes -sa/-salea in their variants -ha/-halea attract stress to the affix's first syllable; ultimate stress in 2-3 syllable words only with heavy final syllables (e.g. /wVt'Vi/ 'ladder', /koko'si/ 'poison frog', verb+PAST -i); Rule 1989 (quoted) reports isolation-form final stress shifting to the first syllable in connected utterances.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms; author notes (via Rule 1989) that stress placement differs between isolation and utterance context, and that stress moves with suffixation. Tone explicitly absent (2.2.1); vowel length (geminate VV) marginally contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Gossner descriptions explicitly treat the Eastern dialect of Edolo (Glottolog east2495; villages Aya, Bobole, Dodomona etc., Komo District, Southern Highlands), which lacks the /n/ phoneme of the Western dialect (west2574). Alternate names: Etoro, Etolo, Edolo Ado.

sources.note: Sec. 2.5 Stress (p.20-21): 'Stress does not appear to fit into any regular pattern.. preference toward penultimate stress.. in agreement with Rule's statement that "stress is unpredictable and in that sense therefore phonemic" (Rule 1989:2). No word pairs.. differentiated only by stress'; 2-syll penult, 3-syll antepenult~penult (penult more common), 4-syll mostly penult; long verbs: stressed syllable changes as suffixes are added, non-primary stresses exist. No phonemic tone.

sources.note: Suprasegmentals (p.3): 'In two syllable words stress nearly always occurs on the first syllable. In three syllable words it seems to vary between being on the first and second syllable with second syllable stress being more common. Four syllable words vary, with the stress most often being on the third syllable but occurring at times on the first or second syllable.' with contrast examples a'baso/'abodo, na'fade/'nagobe, 'nalabali/i'loloba/misi'galë.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2 Stress (p.16-17): no neat pattern; quotes Rule 1989 'stress is unpredictable', fluctuates, final stress in isolation shifts to first syllable in utterances; weak prominence, no minimal pairs, stress moves with suffixation; heavy (CVV) syllables tend to attract stress; 2-syll words nearly always initial/penult; 3-syll penult~antepenult (penult slightly more common), final only if heavy; 4-syll mostly penult; long verbs primary on antepenult/penult with secondary every 2nd-3rd syllable; -ha/-halea attract stress. No tone.
